lessons.title: Word formation: prefixes, suffixes and word families
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — vocabulary, word formation and usage (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the root, prefix and suffix of a word.
Form nouns, adjectives, adverbs and opposites correctly.
Apply the spelling changes that happen when a suffix is added.
reviewNotes: Lists of prefixes and suffixes are common examples, not the complete syllabus list; the teacher may add the items taught in class.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A word is built from a **root** (the main part) with a **prefix** at the front and/or a **suffix** at the end. Knowing these parts helps you to spell, to guess the meaning of new words and to change a word from one class (noun, verb, adjective, adverb) to another. Gap-filling questions in the GCE often ask you to do exactly this.

blocks.title: Prefixes change the meaning
blocks.md:
- **un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis-, non-** = not / the opposite: *unkind, incorrect, impossible, illegal, irregular, disagree*.
- **im-** is used before b, m, p; **il-** before l; **ir-** before r.
- **re-** = again: *rewrite*. **mis-** = wrongly: *misunderstand*. **pre-** = before: *preschool*. **over-** = too much: *overcook*. **under-** = too little: *underpaid*.

blocks.title: Suffixes change the word class
blocks.md:
- **Nouns:** -tion / -sion (*decide → decision*), -ment (*develop → development*), -ness (*kind → kindness*), -ity (*able → ability*), -er / -or (*teach → teacher*), -ship (*friend → friendship*).
- **Adjectives:** -ful (*care → careful*), -less (*care → careless*), -able / -ible, -ous (*danger → dangerous*), -ive, -al.
- **Adverbs:** -ly (*slow → slowly*).
- **Verbs:** -en (*sharp → sharpen*), -ify (*simple → simplify*), -ise.

items.text: A word family from the root 'care'

blocks.caption: One root gives a whole family of words of different classes.
blocks.alt: A diagram with the root care at the top and four arrows pointing to careful (adjective), careless (adjective), carefully (adverb) and carelessness (noun).

blocks.title: Spelling changes when you add a suffix
blocks.md:
1. Final **-y** after a consonant becomes **-i**: *happy → happiness, beauty → beautiful*.
2. Final silent **-e** is usually dropped before a vowel suffix: *hope → hoping*, but kept before a consonant suffix: *hopeful, hopeless*.
3. Short words ending in one vowel + one consonant double the consonant: *begin → beginning, run → runner*.
4. Check the class you need: ask « is a noun, an adjective or an adverb missing here? » before you choose the suffix.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing *carefull* (the suffix is **-ful**, with one l).
- Using the wrong class: *He is a very **success** man* → *successful*; *She sings **beautiful*** → *beautifully*.
- Wrong negative prefix: *unpossible, inpossible* → **impossible**.
- Forgetting that some words keep their form but change class (*to visit / a visit*, *to water / water*).

blocks.title: Example 1: a gap-filling question
blocks.statement: Fill the gap with the correct form of the word in capitals. The ______ of the committee was announced on Friday. (DECIDE)
steps: The gap comes after *The* and before *of*, so a **noun** is needed.
The noun from *decide* uses the suffix -sion: de**cis**ion (the d of decide becomes s).

blocks.title: Example 2: opposites with prefixes
blocks.statement: Give the opposite of: (a) possible (b) regular (c) legal.
steps: Check the first letter of the root: p → **im-**; r → **ir-**; l → **il-**.

lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Choose a synonym or antonym that fits the context.
Explain common idioms and use them correctly.
reviewNotes: The idioms listed are widely used British English idioms; the teacher may replace them with those in the class textbook.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: **Synonyms** are words with nearly the same meaning (*big, large, huge*). **Antonyms** are words with opposite meanings (*generous – mean*). In an exam you must pick the word that fits **the sentence**, not just the dictionary meaning: synonyms are almost never exactly equal.

blocks.title: Choosing the right synonym
blocks.md:
- Same **word class** (a noun is replaced by a noun).
- Same **strength**: *good – excellent – superb* are different degrees.
- Same **register**: *start / begin* (everyday), *commence* (formal); *help* / *assist*; *buy* / *purchase*.
- Same **feeling**: *slim* (positive), *thin* (neutral), *skinny* (negative).
Method: put your word into the sentence and read it again.

items.text: Synonyms of walk: shades of meaning

blocks.caption: The word walk has many synonyms, each with a different shade.
blocks.alt: A centre box with the word walk and four arrows pointing to stroll (slow), march (firm), limp (hurt) and stride (long).

blocks.title: Idioms (1)
blocks.md:
An **idiom** is a fixed expression whose meaning is not the sum of its words.
- **a piece of cake** = very easy
- **break the ice** = make people feel relaxed at a first meeting
- **under the weather** = slightly ill
- **spill the beans** = reveal a secret
- **let the cat out of the bag** = reveal a secret by mistake

blocks.title: Idioms (2)
blocks.md:
- **once in a blue moon** = very rarely
- **hit the nail on the head** = say exactly the right thing
- **bite the bullet** = accept something unpleasant bravely
- **the last straw** = the final problem that makes a situation unbearable
- **cost an arm and a leg** = be very expensive

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Translating an idiom word for word from your mother tongue: it must keep its exact English words (*a piece of cake*, not *a slice of cake*).
- Taking the idiom literally in a comprehension question.
- Using many idioms in one essay: one or two well-chosen ones are enough.
- Choosing an antonym of the wrong word class or sense.

blocks.title: Example 1: a synonym in context
blocks.statement: *The principal was furious when the pupils broke the window.* Choose the closest meaning of *furious*: (a) very angry (b) slightly worried (c) surprised.
steps: (b) is too weak and (c) describes another feeling.

blocks.title: Example 2: an idiom
blocks.statement: *Nkeng told me about the surprise party and I almost let the cat out of the bag.* What did the speaker nearly do?
steps: The idiom *let the cat out of the bag* means to reveal a secret by mistake.
So the speaker nearly told someone about the surprise party.
blocks.answer: He or she nearly revealed the secret.

lessons.title: Words often confused
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — vocabulary, word formation and usage (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Choose between look-alike and sound-alike words.
Use a quick test for each pair.
reviewNotes: British spelling is used (practise as verb); the teacher should confirm the convention expected by the GCE Board.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: Many mistakes in exam scripts come from pairs of words that look or sound alike. Learn them in **pairs with a short example**, and build your own memory trick.

blocks.title: Pairs (1)
blocks.md:
- **affect** (verb: to influence) / **effect** (noun: a result). *Drought affects crops. The effect is hunger.*
- **advice** (noun) / **advise** (verb). *She gave me advice. She advised me.*
- **practice** (noun) / **practise** (verb, British spelling). *Football practice. We practise daily.*
- **principal** (head of a school; main) / **principle** (a rule or belief).
- **lose** (to misplace) / **loose** (not tight).

blocks.title: Pairs (2)
blocks.md:
- **accept** (receive) / **except** (apart from).
- **stationary** (not moving) / **stationery** (paper, pens).
- **quiet** (silent) / **quite** (fairly).
- **complement** (to complete) / **compliment** (a kind remark).
- **borrow** (take for a while) / **lend** (give for a while). *Lend me your pen* = I take it; *I borrowed his pen*.
- **bring** (towards here) / **take** (away from here).

blocks.title: Pairs (3)
blocks.md:
- **fewer** (things you can count: *fewer pupils*) / **less** (things you cannot count: *less water*).
- **between** (two) / **among** (three or more).
- **their** (belonging to them) / **there** (place) / **they're** (they are).
- **its** (belonging to it) / **it's** (it is or it has).
- **your** (belonging to you) / **you're** (you are).
- **whose** (belonging to whom) / **who's** (who is).

blocks.caption: A quick test: if you can put a, an or the in front of the word, use the noun, effect.
blocks.alt: A small table with three columns. Row one: affect, verb, to influence. Row two: effect, noun, a result.

blocks.title: Quick tests
blocks.md:
- Can you put **the / an** before the word? Then it is the **noun** (advice, effect, practice).
- **its / it's**: replace with *it is*. If the sentence still works, write **it's**.
- **fewer / less**: can you count them? Then **fewer**.
- **lose / loose**: *lose* has the sound of « looz »; *loose* is the opposite of *tight*.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *The teacher gave us an advice.* (advice cannot take *an* or a plural).
- *Don't loose your ticket.* → lose.
- *It's wheels are broken.* → its.
- *There were less pupils.* → fewer.
- *Everybody accept Ali came.* → except.

blocks.title: Example 1: affect or effect
blocks.statement: *The heavy rain ______ the road to Bamenda.* Choose: affected / effect.
steps: The gap needs a **verb** (the rain did something to the road).
The verb is *affected*; *effect* is a noun.

blocks.title: Example 2: accept or except
blocks.statement: *Everyone ______ Tabe came to the meeting.* Choose: accept / except.
steps: The word means « apart from » so it must be *except*.
*Accept* is a verb meaning to receive.

lessons.title: Cameroon English and standard English: common pitfalls
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — vocabulary, word formation and usage (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Recognise frequent errors heard in everyday speech.
Replace them with standard written English.
Understand why the exam expects standard English.
reviewNotes: The expressions are based on widely observed learner errors in West African and Cameroonian English; a Cameroonian English teacher must confirm the list and the examples. Items such as stay/live and open/close the light depend on regional usage: kept as advice for the exam only.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: English in Cameroon is rich and has its own colour: expressions, rhythm and words of local origin. It is a living variety. But the GCE marks **standard written English**, which is understood everywhere. This lesson lists frequent slips that cost marks.

blocks.title: Grammar slips (1)
blocks.md:
- *She has lived here **since** five years* → **for** five years (**since** + a starting point: *since 2019*; **for** + a length of time).
- *We discussed **about** the problem* → *discussed the problem*. Same with *return back* → *return*, *emphasise on* → *emphasise*, *cope up with* → *cope with*.
- *informations, advices, furnitures, equipments, luggages* → these are **uncountable**: *information, advice, furniture, equipment, luggage* (say *a piece of advice*).

blocks.title: Grammar slips (2)
blocks.md:
- **State verbs** are not used in the continuous: *I am knowing* → **I know**; *He is having a car* → **He has**; also *want, like, understand, believe, belong*.
- **Repeated subject:** *My mother she sells fish* → **My mother sells fish.** One subject, one pronoun at most.
- **Prepositions:** *congratulate somebody **on***, *depend **on***, *different **from***, *listen **to***.

blocks.title: Word choice
blocks.md:
- *Borrow me your pen* → **Lend me your pen** (or: *May I borrow your pen?*).
- *Open / close the light* → **switch on / switch off** the light.
- *Where do you stay?* is understood locally; in an exam write **Where do you live?** for a permanent home.
- Local words (names of dishes, titles) are fine in a story or a letter if the reader will understand, but not for general vocabulary in formal essays.

blocks.caption: Five frequent slips and their standard form.
blocks.alt: A two-column table. Left column: discuss about it, return back, an advice, I am knowing, borrow me a pen. Right column: discuss it, return, a piece of advice, I know, lend me a pen.

blocks.title: How to correct yourself
blocks.md:
1. Read your answer slowly and look at **prepositions** and **verb forms** first.
2. Ask: is this word **countable**?
3. Ask: is this verb a **state** verb?
4. Does the sentence have a **doubled subject**?
5. In speech, relax and be natural; in the exam, **check** these points.

blocks.title: Common mistakes (even after correction)
blocks.md:
- Over-correcting: *I look forward to **see** you* is wrong; the form is *to seeing* (look forward **to** + -ing).
- Writing *since two weeks* in a letter.
- Using speech-style short forms (*gonna, wanna*) in formal writing.
- Mixing standard and non-standard forms in the same paragraph.

blocks.title: Example 1: correcting a sentence
blocks.statement: Correct: *My brother he is having many informations about the scholarship.*
blocks.answer: My brother has a lot of information about the scholarship.

blocks.title: Example 2: since or for
blocks.statement: Complete: *We have been waiting at the garage ______ two hours.*
steps: Two hours is a **length of time**.
